subtopic: PROPOSED FOREST RESERVE IN SPIRIT RIVER DISTRICT.

speechtext: On the Orders of the Day:

subtopic: PROPOSED FOREST RESERVE IN SPIRIT RIVER DISTRICT.
speechtext: The Minister of the Interior is not here, but I desire to ask for information, and no doubt the minister will be good enough to give it later. I have received a somewhat lengthy night lettergram from the secretary of the Spirit River Board of Trade protesting against the prospective setting apart of a forest reserve in that vicinity, and asserting on what is claimed to be good authority that at least 50 per cent of the land is clear, the soil good, good water available, and the balance of the land very light scrub. It is said that several whole sections can be ploughed without any previous preparation and that there is no muskeg. The land is in township 79-81, ranges 7-11 inclusive. I shall be glad if the hon. minister will say whether or not it is the intention to establish a forest reserve in that section of the country.
On the Orders of the Day:

During the consideration of the Orders in Council of the Department of the Interior that took place in the House some days ago, in discussing a certain order regarding homestead entry by volunteers, the Minister of the Interior spoke as follows:
With regard to the protection of the homesteading rights of those who have enlisted, I think the hon. gentleman has probably misinterpreted the Order in Council. He states that we are giving practically the same protection to the soldier who has made his homestead entry after enlistment as we are giving to the man who was the owner of a homestead prior to enlistment. But there is a difference in our treatment of these two men. The man who had a homestead prior to enlistment has not only protection in so far as not allowing cancellation proceedings to be instituted, but he is also allowed to count as time of residence on his homestead the time that he is serving his country at the front. In the case of the volunteer who makes a homestead entry after enlistment, he is not allowed to count his time but he is protected from cancellation.
I find in the Manitoba Free Press of May 3, under the heading "Homestead for Every Soldier," an article which copies an announcement said to have been made by the Department of Militia with regard to this particular matter. The Militia Department apparently holds an entirely different view from that held by the Minister of the Interior, and it is this difference of view that I desire to bring to the attention of the House with a view to having the two divergent views harmonized; otherwise there will be misunderstanding and unfortunate consequences. I shall not read the whole article, but the important part is as follows:
The scope of the Act in the foregoing particulars has been enlarged to embrace volunteers who may, subsequent to the date of enlistment, enter for a homestead of Dominion lands. By the operation of the new regulation the Minister of the Interior is empowered to consider the latter class of soldier settlers in the same way as the Act provides for the bona fide settler, who, on the outbreak of hostilities, enlisted for active service.
Who makes the statement?

The newspaper credits it to new regulations of the Militia Department. I will read what it says:
The new regulations affecting this matter are contained in Militia orders issued at Ottawa.
I think ,it is very desirable that the House should be informed as to the divergent views expressed, and, whatever is the intention, certainly it should be understood distinctly from the beginning.

(Laprairie-Napier-ville) (Translation.) Mr. Speaker, before the motion carries, I wish once more to record a protest against this mad policy, which is bound to bring ruin to the country. True it is that I stand alone in this House in the position I am taking, but I count more sympathizers outside this House than within its precincts, and I shall name one of them especially: he is Baron Shaugh-nessy. At a meeting of the manufacturers of the Montreal district, held only a few months ago at the Montread Board of Trade, speaking in the presence of General Sir Sam Hughes, the Baron stated that the Government ought, without delay, to put a stop to recruiting, because, he said, we already have 135,000 men under arms, and it will take twelve to fifteen months before those soldiers are sent overseas. He said, furthermore, that in discontinuing now such recruiting campaigns a monthly expenditure of five to six millions would be saved to Canada. He predicted that the economical situation would become more and more tense; that this country will soon have no more hands to till the land. In proof of his argument, he stated, in the presence of the Minister of Militia that the western farmers hfid called upon him to bring them, if possible, 10,000 men for sowing time.
During the last twenty-one months, Mr. Speaker, the Government has sent overseas -I mean to France and Belgium-65,000 solldiers. More than 70,000 are in training camps in England, while the rest are being trained in Canadian camps. If the Government continues the methods they have followed to this day for sending soldiers overseas, and if they insist on carrying through a levy of 500,000 troops, I find, by an easy computation, that it will take them over ten years to carry 500,000 men to the front.
I fail to see, taking the situation such as it is, why the Government should drag the people of this country into bankruptcy against its wish by persevering in a policy of unnecessary enlistment. So far as I am 
concerned, any discussion on this subject would be wasted time; to me the question is as clear as crystal. If it has been possible for France to hold more than 400 miles of trenches with her 39 millions of inhabitants, I wish to know how it is that England, with a greater interest than ours in this war, cannot take care of more than 40 miles of trenches, when her population is 49 millions.

(Translation.) With my hon. friend's leave, I wish to state that the British army is now taking care, not of 35 to 40 miles of trenches, but of a good deal over 100 miles. My hon. friend is mistaken, because the British line now extends over 100 miles.

(Translation.) The minister who has just interrupted me has his own source of information, which I feel not like questioning; but I have my own information, and I hope he will not question it either.
But I must say that only lately the British army extended over only 35 miles, and they have now taken care of five more' miles. I do not care to name the gentleman who has given me this information, because he had no authority to do so. But granted that the British line had 100 miles of trenches to defend, if only one-tenth of the truth has been given out by newspapers since the beginning of this war, when they stated that Britain had from three to four millions of soldiers undier arms, I fail to see where they have been sent. If little France, with its population of 39 millions, as I have stated, could take charge of 400 miles of trenches, Britain, with the help of its dominions, such as Australia, Canada and New' Zealand, should at least be able to take care of her 100 miles of trenches', which is stated by the Postmaster General as the extent of her line, although I beg to differ with him on that score, as I claim it is at the utmost 40 miles. But in any case that is not the point I wish ,to make.
The other day, in this House, the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark) stated that we should not let our thoughts, wander from the war. It seems as if his mind was filled with the idea and he will not speak of anything else. The hon. member might take a trip overseas and get a line on what is being done in England. He then could give good advice to our British friends, who have more dissensions to contend with than

[DOT]we have, and he might show them how to carry on their business better than it is carried on to-day.
I wish to quote, as agreeing with what I have to say, the words of the hon. member for North Simcoe (Mr. Currie) who spoke in this House in the afternoon of the 22nd of February last, while I spoke that same evening. He was congratulating the right hon. the leader of the Opposition and the Liberal party for refraining from any party politics in Canada, while he stated the practice was current in Britain. If the hon. . member for Red Deer is horrified at what is taking place in this House, I should advise him, as he has been in Canada only a few years from the Old Country, to take a trip to Britain to find out what is going on and endeavour to suggest to the British Government some means of recruiting soldiers to light in the trenches of France and Belgium.
Since the outbreak of the war we have been following in the footsteps of the old countries of Europe, of countries which have accumulated wealth for ages, while the truth is that we are mere beggars compared with European nations. Every dollar required to foot our war bill we have to borrow, while Britain has money loaned in all parts of the world. But we, the scions of Britain, in our need, we are going to borrow this year $300,000,000 to 400,000,000 to carry on the war and cover the deficit in our ordinary and special expenditures.
What is our daily war expenditure in Canada? Only a few weeks ago the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) enquired from the Minister of Finance what we were spending monthly for war purposes. The reply was that the expenses reached from ten to eleven millions, or $300,000 to $400,000 per day.
Now, referring to the Canada Gazette of the 15th of April last, I find that the expenditure for March totals more than twice the amount stated in this House by the Minister o'f Finance. For that one month it reached over $25,000,000. So that if we keep on spending as lavishly and recruiting day after day, as has been done since the opening of hostilities, of course we must expect the expenses to keep on the increase.
At that rate, according to my computation, the war expenses for the year will total $300,000,000.
But, Mr. Speaker, our obligations after the war are not confined to those figures. The Minister of Finance has stated that after the war we shall have to make adjustments for ammunition, supplies and
clothing; well, what about our share of the cost? Will it be $100,000,000 or $200,000,000? I cannot tell. But, Mr. Speaker, if we are to judge from the prices paid for shells and fuses, articles that come high both in Canada and in the United States, when this Government is the purchaser, it must be admitted that our share of the expenses will be large. Furthermore, the time will come when we shall have to provide for many other things in Canada, such as our railways for instance, for which even at this session we have been asked to provide.
I forgot to state that the expenditure for the country's management, only the ordinary and special accounts, will reach $217,000,000; the war account will total up to $300,000,000, or an aggregate expenditure of 517 millions for a population of 7) millions of people and a revenue of $170,000,000. There will at that rate be a deficit in the expense account of $330,000,000 over revenue, or $65 to $70 per unit of population.
Yet the press will go on clamouring that our duty is to run to the rescue of the Empire. I am fully disposed, indeed, to save the Empire, I have no objection whatever to run to her rescue, but the Solicitor General (Mr. Meighen) ought not to be taken at his word when he advised last year the people of Manitoba to drive the country into bankruptcy against the wish of its citizens; yet I think this Government has followed very closely the Solicitor General's advice. However, Mr. Speaker, when you see that the people are thus badly misinformed, when public opinion is perverted by the public press here as well as in England and all over, the day is coming when a reaction will set in, and the same people who have been shamefully deceived by the politicians of 1915, 1916 and 1917, will wreak a terrible vengeance on its deceivers. [DOT]
As a member of' this House, I want to keep my electors posted on what is going on here and in that connection I must say that over in England there is a man I admire more than all other public men of Britain or of any country in the world. I mean Llovd-George who again and again in the British Commons, has disclosed what Great Britain has done and what she has failed to do. I admit in passing that the British navy has done a great deal; but, as stated by Lloyd-George, it must be conceded that Great Britain has scarcely done anything on land. . In a notable speech in the

House of Commons, the British minister inquired of his colleagues what part the British had taken in the struggle? France, said he, has been fighting for the past 18 months against one half of the German host. Russia with practically no arms and no munitions has held her own against the other half of the German enemy, against the whole Austrian army, the Bulgarians and the Turks. And what have we done? Nothing. Such are his very words.
Those are the words of a statesman. A statesman should always tell his people the truth. Why, in this country should we not tell the people that the policy which has been adopted by this Parliament will be disastrous, and can be carried out only by increased taxation on revenue and property. What good purpose is served by the newspapers spreading the hope of better times, after the war? Who can claim that now, when we know that after the war our purchasing power will be cut down by a million and a half per day so as to keep our soldiers in the cities, what doing? I would rather not speak of it in this House. I am really shocked when I see what is going on here and in Montreal. A large number of these young men go from one saloon to another and get drunk. It is perfectly well known that the training the soldiers get here is of no value whatever to them, that when they get to England, they have to go through their training all over again. If such be the case, why keep on recruiting? Why should these young men from the country be kept in the cities and get the habit of drink and immorality. I say it is high time to put a stop to that. If in six or twelve months, the soldiers that have already enlisted must be sent overseas; if it is hoped that by shipping to the front the few thousand soldiers which are being trained, the Empire will be saved, so much the better; it ought to be done and I shall not object. [DOT] But there is as yet no evidence that your idea is the Empire's safety. Why do you not acknowledge, as men should do who speak their minds, that your purpose in recruiting is to promote jingoism pure and simple.
In my constituency, I tell you that not five per cent of the people approve of your present policy. Then go into the rural districts throughout the country and you will realize that your system of enlistment is not in the least favoured by the nation at large. I must state to the House that I am now speaking for myself only, and that when anybody rises to speak on this ques-

tion on behalf of the Liberal party, he does not express my opinion. My position in this matter is my own.
I do not wish to delay the House. As I have stated, the Government will have to take over the railways. The Canadian Northern has an indebtedness of $420,000,000, besides loans in practically all the banks of the country. We must also operate the National Transcontinental, which will increase out burden by $700,000,000. The public debt, in round numbers, is to-day $920,000,000, and with the expected deficit of $300,000,000 by the 3tst of March, 1917, it will reach $2,000,000,000. And to what purpose? What have we to show for that inordinate expenditure, over which the people have no control? Absolutely nothing. We have sent our soldiers into the trenches to have them butchered, while at the beginning of the waT we could not provide them -with rifles and ammunition. Why keep to that policy? Within the current year we shall have to pay $100,000,000 in interest. Furthermore, we shall have to provide pensions for the invalids, the widows and the orphans, likely amounting to $30,000,000 or $40,000,000. We shall also have to provide for the different commissions which this Government is creating every day out of a revenue which will decrease after the war by several millions on account of the lowering of the country's purchasing power, as I explained a while ago.
I say, then, that conditions after the war will not be as rosy in this country as editors would have us believe.
I stated already that, in so far as I was concerned, I want to put these facts and the true situation, as I understand it, before the people of this country, and more especially of my county. My purpose is not to court popularity; I do it from a sense of duty, prompted by my conscience, because the people have been misinformed, and because the politicians who owe their election to their stand against all military expenditure, against the naval proposals, and against all contributions to Imperial defence, ought to have joined me in my protest in this House when I say to the Government: If you want to go into such follies first get the people's assent to them.
Mr. Speaker, as I have alluded to the navy and to dreadnoughts, I will say that I have often listened to the right hon. Prime Minister as he spoke to us of dreadnoughts and of the Senate's refusal-the naughty Senate-to vote for the famous

Bill to contribute three dreadnoughts to the Imperial defence. Much was said of the German menace. But the Prime Minister went to Great Britain; why, then, did he not warn the British Government of how imminent was the German menace and not urge them to increased preparedness?
If Great Britain was not ready when the war broke out, why should Canada have been in greater readiness? One must use his common sense.
I congratulate the Senate for having saved to the country the cost at least of the three dreadnoughts. Since the English fleet is keeping the German fleet bottled up, of what advantage would it be for Great Britain to have three more dreadnoughts in the North sea, or elsewhere?
Mr. Speaker, I shall not take up the time of the House any further. I have already discussed the question, and I shall do so every time it comes before the House in the same spirit as I speak of it at home. I intend objecting as strongly as I know how against that disastrous policy, and if anyone saw fit to bring in an amendment to reduce that amount by 100 millions I should vote for it.

speechtext:
Certainly, my
hon. friend can discuss anything he thinks desirable.

There is one point I
would like to bring up. The country is spending a lot of money on training young officers, and I saw it stated the other day by a colonel in charge of a regiment in the West, I think, that there were enough young officers now training, to whom the Government had not been able to give positions, to man at least two battalions. That would mean 2,000 men who had qualified for commissions, but to whom there were no commissions to give. The acting minister stated last night, I think, that,, as far as possible, it was the intention, and I think rightly, in granting commissions in future to give them to men who had served at the front and in the ranks. It would seem to me that something ought to be done either to stop the expenditure in training young officers, when we have so
many that we cannot use, or to see that the services of those young officers are utilized. The Government have expended a considerable amount of money on training officers, and if it be true that there are at least 2,000 of them who cannot be used, something should be done. If they cannot be used as officers, why can they not go to the front as privates or a3 non-commissioned officers? I know numbers of them have been qualified for over a year, and have been waiting to go to the front, but they have not gone, and apparently are not going. It looks to me a3 if many of those officers did not want to go as privates, and so the country is going to lose their services altogether. I do not suppose that it is altogether their fault. It is quite natural that a young man should want to go a3 an officer if he can secure a position, but if there are no positions to give, something ought to be done, either to shut off the expense of training more officers, or to see that those who have qualified give their services to the country in some capacity.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: T do not think that the spirit which my hon. friend seems to have found is one that prevails to any extent. On the contrary, it has been the experience of the Department of Militia and Defence that men have been willing to waive their rank and go to the front in a lower rank. [DOT]
In some cases, yes.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
More than that, there have been many cases where men holding commissions and rank in the Militia have put them to one side and gone to the front as privates; so that any such aspersion as my hon. friend seems to be inclined to pass upon the young men of the country is altogether unfounded and unwarranted. The experience of the department is that any young man who desires to take a course as an officer will certainly not be the worse for that if he does go to the front. Further than that, the regulations of the de-' partment are that in all the training schools throughout Canada the men who shall have precedence are the men who have first volunteered for service overseas. The Canadian force of 300,000 requires, I think, about 10,000 officers. These young men are being trained in schools which are kept up for that purpose, and up to the .present we have not found any detrimental results from keeping these schools open. The deputy minister informs me that while the young men are training in these schools,



they receive only the remuneration of ordinary privates.

I do not think that the Prime Minister is justified in the tone of criticism which he has adopted towards me for bringing up this matter. I got the information from one of his own officers, and it was published broadcast throughout the country that thete were over 2,000 of those men who could not 'be used as; officers. I do not see any harm in pointing out a matter like that to the department. If this officer has not given proper information to the country, that is not my fault.

I have already had an
opportunity during the present session of' putting a question to the Prime Minister regarding recruiting. Canadians generally are very anxious' to give to the Emipre all the assistance possible in this great war, but when the announcement was made by the Prime Minister that 500,000 men would be recruited, compulsory service had not been adopted in England. Now that the conditions in England have changed, I would ask whether he thinks it will be necessary to go to the full extent of recruiting 500,000 Canadians. We have been told by some very reliable authorities that this could only be done by seriously affecting the economic services of the country, and we can all realize, with our limited population, what 500,000 men leaving the country would mean. With the conditions now changed in England, and, in view of the new legislation adopted there, does the right hon. gentleman think it would be still necessary to recruit 500,000 Canadians?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council

What my hon. friend suggests, I understand, is that because Great Britain is proposing to do more, we ought to take into consideration the desirability of doing less than we at first proposed. We have not taken that into consideration, and we do not intend to depart from the announcement that was made on the first day of January.

Post Office-to provide for the payment of one year's salary to the widow of John Lina-hen, railway mail clerk, Montreal district, who died on the 22nd March, 1914, from pneumonia, which he contracted while on duty, $800.
What is the explanation of this?

On the 23rd of February, 1914, John Linahen was asked to go out on a special postal car with a large quantity of mail matter that had been left over at BonaventuTe station, Montreal, on account of a storm. The deor of this car would not close on account of the ice, and Linahen protested against the state of the car, but finally consented to go. He caught

a chill while on the car and contracted pneumonia, of which he died a short time afterwards. As he had contracted this while on duty the department thought it only right to grant a compassionate allowance to his widow.

I do not object to his widow receiving a compassionate allowance, but I think my hon. friend, who is a good lawyer, will agree with me that an action could be brought against the company. The railway company provides the mail cars, and has to keep them heated and in a proper condition. As a lawyer, who was in practice some years ago, I would venture the opinion very modestly that the widow has a claim against the company, but not against the department.

Strictly speaking, that may be so. A case similar to this occurred last year. This is what the officers of the
department say on Linahenfs case:
There was no heat in this car. The doors could not he closed on account of ice on the floor. The steam coils were inoperative on account of the cold, and it was three or four hours after the train started before it was possible to get the door closed.
It may be true that technically the widow has a claim against the railway company, _ but I doubt very much whether she would be able to recover, or whether it would pay the Government to take action against the company. There was no faijlt on the man's part, and I think we are only doing what is right in granting his widow this allowance.

There is no objection at all to the allowance being granted, for the case seems to be a deserving one. But I see in these Estimates half a dozen, if not a full dozen, oases of a similar nature. All these may be meritorious, but I never saw the Estimates so loaded up as they are this year with items of this character. Is there any rule followed by the Government as to granting gratuities? The country is, of course, disposed to deal generously with public servants who lose their health or their life in the service, but there ought to be some rule in cases of this kind, and I would particularly call the attention of the Minister of Trade and Commerce to this matter, because he was very severe on this point in times gone by.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I do not know that I can say much more than has been said by the Prime Minister. I first approached the question rather with the idea of applying in each province to our employees the Compensation Act of that province; but as the Prime Minister has pointed out, we found that that would produce the result that, as our employees are scattered throughout the Dominion and as the accidents that might happen to them resulting in death or in injury, would happen under very similar circumstances, if a man happened to be in one province, we would be paying him less than if he happened to be in another province. What calls for some consideration is whether we should select the system used in some one province and make it for our purposes generally applicable, or whether we should make something of a compromise of the different rules laid down in the various provinces and make that apply generally to our employees who may suffer injury or death in the performance of their duties, so that they will find themselves in the same position towards the Government as that in which an ordinary employee finds himself towards his employer under a General Compensation Act. I think the proper course would be for us to adopt a system of our own, selecting the most commendable features of 
the different Acts, and then we would be in a position to treat all our employees in all parts of the Dominion upon the same basis.
Sir WILFRID ^LAURIER: I repeat that the matter should be dealt with systematically, and the system ought to be that any servant of the Government who meets injury or death in the performance of his duty is entitled to compensation. The rate of compensation should be according to his salary. That is the Tule adopted generally, and, I think, if adopted by the Government, it would meet the requirements of the case. We must have a system of our ora, and the Minister of Justice, by comparing the different systems, can come to some decision. Instead of these different payments being placed in the Supplementary Estimates, if they are to be made at all, they ought to be made under a well understood system.

I have something to
say about other gratuities, but I shall wait until we xeach the Supplementary Estimates.

It is true that the different provinces have Compensation Acts by which they allot to those who are injured varying amounts according to degree of injury. Inasmuch as this is a matter within the control of the provinces, I think the proper course would be to deal with each case under the Compensation Act of the province in which the accident occurred. It is true that you have the anomaly that a man who suffered injury or death would secure more for himself in case of injury and for his wife and children in case of death if he happened to be in one province than in another, but such things are bound to occur. The railways operate in the different provinces and they settle the claims that arise in each province according to the rules laid down by the legislature of that province, and I do not think any one considers that to be an anomaly or that that system should be done away with. Inasmuch as the matter is one of provincial concern, and a matter in which the province settles the quantum in respect of all the circumstances in the province in which the injured party lives, it may be right that the system should be a varying one. Perhaps in British Columbia a larger sum might be art equitable and just settlement that in one of the eastern provinces where living is much cheaper. I do not

think he blanket rate would be the best one. The Minister of Trade and Commerce can bear me out that some months ago I presented this view to him in a friendly way, in the same way as I am making these remarks now, and he has been good enough 1 to give the matter consideration, although no decision has yet been arrived at. The matter concerned the employees, in our government grain elevators, in which men in my own town have been injured; and one at least killed. If they are working for the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, or the Ogilvie Elevator Company, or any of the other elevator companies, they get compensation under the Workmen's Compensation Act. Surely, none of us who are voting the public money would wish our employees to be treated less generously than the employees of those companies, and it seems that the most simple and just way would be to extend the Exchequer Court Act to give the judge of that court power to deal with the matter, and if he thinks fit, to take cognizance of the Workmen's Compensation Act of the province in which the matter arises. Whether or not the Exchequer Court Act would have to be amended would be for the Minister of Justice to decide. If a province has not a Compensation Act, that is its own business, because it has its provincial rights and is supreme in that sphere. Just as the Canadian Pacific Railway Company is a business concern and conducts its business throughout the various provinces, complying with the legislation in the respective provinces as such legislation affects its business, so this Dominion Government should act, and I would be pleased if some such arrangement could be arrived at in the near future.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The hon. member for Moosejaw (Mr. Knowles) made inquiry as to punishment administered to certain privates of the 128th overseas, battalion. As the hon. member was not here yesterday, I might repeat what I said with regard to the administration of field punishment No. 1:
Although there is nothing in our Canadian regulations dealing with the subject matter, the British regulations entitled " Manual of Military Daw" page 721, deals with field punishment. Sub-paragraph (d) of paragraph (a) reads:	''When in irons a soldier may be
attached for a period or periods not exceeding two hours of any one day to a fixed object, but he must not be so attached during more
than three of any four consecutive days, nor during more than twenty-one days in all."
The memorandum which I have before me continues:
Our officers commanding have applied this regulation notwithstanding the fact that it is no more applied in the British army. They have done it through ignorance and over zeal. The Adjutant General has given instructions that all kinds of field punishment, excepting detention, are not to be applied for the future.
It is therefore hoped that there will be no further recurrence of incidents of this kind. So far as the particular case is concerned, the Teport that .we have, after investigation by the Provost-Marshal, is as follows. It comes from the District Officer commanding military district No. 1:
Reference Adjutant-General's wire 27th instant and further reference my reply same date are field punishment being administered by O.C. 128th Overseas Battalion. Case has been investigated by Provost-Marshall who reports that Privates Anderson and Graham whilst undergoing detention were given field punishment No. 1 for a period of approximately fifty minutes at the expiration of which time medical officer reported no bad effects. The Provost-Marshall's investigation also brought out the fact that Rieut.-Colonel Hawlett has administered on different occasions field punishment in a mild form. Full explanation was however made to him with reference to this form of punishment and instructions given him that it was to be discontinued at once and that in future he was to award detention instead. From the Provost-Marshall's investigation it would seem that aggravated cases only were dealt with in this manner. Please advise me if you wish any further action in this connection.

I am very thankful to the Prime Minister for having had thie matter looked into. I am quite sure he would be even more opposed to cruelty to any soldier than I would.. We have had the matter cleared up so that there will be no shadow over the regiment on thie account, and this form of punishment will be stopped. Therefore the purpose of the inquiry has been attained. The Prime Minister spoke of only two soldiers, but the names of three were given. I suppose that is not worth bothering very much about.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Only two are mentioned, but as other cases are alluded to I imagine that all have been considered.

I assume so. I should like to know where these boys are now. I am told that pending this investigation two of them were taken out of Moosejaw and put into the Regina 68th, then on the eve of departure, and that they are now across the ocean. If that is correct, of course their evidence could not have been taken.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I really have * no information on that point, hut I will make inquiry.

I do not ask for that. I trust the regiment in Mooeejaw will be even more successful than it has been and that the bringing of this matter before Parliament in this way will .have a good effect. I understand that these are the only cases in Canada in which an officer has administered this punishment.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No. I explained that there was a case in Trenton, N.S., where the same punishment was administered. An investigation was held, and the same direction was given to the commanding officer. Indeed, .the directions have been made general to all commanding officers in Canada, that this form of punishment shall not be administered in the future. I entirely agree with the Adjutant General that these instructions should be issued. It will be the duty of the proper officer of the Militia Department to see that these instructions are carried out.
In this field punishment No. 1, are the arms suspended above the head?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
It is expressed in general terms in what I read a moment ago:	_
When in irons a soldier may be attached for a period or periods not exceeding two hours of any one day to a fixed object, but he must not be so attached during more than three of any four consecutive days, nor during more than twenty-one days In all.
My hon. friend will find in Hansard of yesterday an account of the punishment administered to a soldier in Trenton. His feet rested on the ground but his hands were attached to an object above his head. He remained in that position for an hour. There were no ill physical effects except that, as he stated himself, his arms felt quite tired. There is no particular description in the report of the officer commanding military district No. 10, but only the general reference to field punishment which I have read.
The rumour which I reported to the Prime Minister to the effect that the man had fainted 'is neither confirmed nor denied?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
That rumour would hardly be consistent with the report of the officer, to the effect that these soldiers were given this punishment for

a period of approximately fifty minutes, at the end of which time the medical officer reported no bad effects.

Are any other punishments provided for offences on the part of Canadian soldiers?
Sir ROBtERT BORDEN: The order given out is that they shall be punished by detention, but not in any other way.
I desire to make answer to a question asked of me by the hon. member for Regina <Mr. W. M. Martin) with reference to the case of Private Darrach of the 68th overseas battalion, who was in the hospital and who died, and the members of whose family were not present in time to see him before his death. The report which I have from the AdjutantjGeneral, which is addressed to the deputy minister, is as follows:
With reference to your minute of the 2nd 'instant, attached herewith, it is pointed out that a report was called for some time ago regarding this matter.
On April 4, the Officer Commanding Military District No. 10 forwarded a copy of a letter from the Grey Nuns' Hospital, Regina, which states in part:
" X must admit that there was a complaint from the parents of Private Darrach. But when the .patient arrived at the hospital hiis condition was that of an ordinary influenza case, his temperature being 101 degrees raising to 104 degrees, and again coming down to the same point, with no other complications. The next morning his condition changed for the worse, shortly before his death, hardly giving us time to notify the doctor and the family, these taking a whole hour before reaching the hospital. In this case we understand that the parents must have felt very much grieved, and this excited them to lay the said complaint; but any one who saw the patient and ourselves were just as astonished at the sudden turn, which could not have been prevented."
The description of this man's illness and death as taken from the official medical board, held on January 29 last, at Regina, substantiates the report from the hospital as to the fact that this man's death was very sudden, and that up to the hour before his death he was not considered to be seriously ill. The report is as follows:
" That he was taken sick on January 24, 1916, and was given usual treatment for La Grippe.
That condition did not improve and he was admitted to barracks hospital at 4 p.m. Tuesday, January 25, 1916, and was seen by Captain Morrison about 6.30 p.m., when he was detained in hospital and treatment continued.
That on January 26, 1916, at the hour of 9.30 he was examined by Captain Coles and treatment continued; temperature, a.m., 101-5.
Temperature p.m., 102-6. As his condition remained unimproved on this evening he was removed to Grey Nuns' Hospital at 7 p.m. After being placed in bed it was found that his temperature was 101-4.

That he was examined by Doctor Wallace at 11 a.m., January 2T,	1916, when it was
found that influenza was present, but gradually becoming worse. Temperature, 7 a.m., 104-2; pulse, 100 ; respiration, 24.
The disease pursued the usual course until 11 a.m., January 28, 1916, when heart failed. He became cyanosed. Pulse became imperceptible and he died at 12 a.m. same date in spite of temperature 100-4, pulse 90, respiration 30."
(Sgd.) W. E. Hodgins,
Major-General,
Adjutant-General.

It seems to me that when his temperature was ranging up to 104 there was great carelessness on the part of the Militia authorities or of the doctors in charge that this man's people were not notified. I wonder what degree of temperature would be necessary before they would notify the relatives? The report that the temperature went up to 104 degrees carries condemnation on its face. Any one who knows anything about fevers or about temperatures knows that his relatives should have been notified when he was in that condition.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The temperature does seem to have been very high.
There is absolutely no excuse for a thing like that.

In reference to the punishments inflicted, no doubt the committee highly approves the decision of the Government not to permit such punishment in future. May I ask whether any consideration has been given to the officers who inflicted these punishments?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I have not con suited the Adjutant General with regard to that; there has not been an opportunity of doing so. The punishments were authorized under the British War Office regulations, which are applicable to our force. It is not usual to administer such punishments in Great Britain, and they will not be administered here in the future. 'The punishments do not seem to have been attended with any ill effects to the physique of the young men, and I do not know under the circumstances whether the Adjutant General would recommend any disciplining of the officers or not. I shall, however, consult him as to that.

I take the opportunity of expressing the opinion that while the officers had the authority of the regulations enabling them to inflict this punishment, the fact that the regulation had become obsolete in Great Britain was evidence of
a change in conditions and opinions that . an officer properly appreciating. his position and responsibilities would surely have taken notice of. In Canada, where conditions are so far removed from those that prevail in military circles in England, an officer who would exercise the authority given by the regulations to that extent would seem to have shown that he was not the man for the position; that there was error in judgment in placing him in that position, or that, at any rate, after his having committed that error in judgment it would be a mistake to continue him in the position. It is not possible to lay down rules and regulations for the conduct of officers, especially commanding officers under all circumstances. If an officer does not show that he has judgment over and above what is laid down in the regulations, it seems to me that he demonstrates that he is not the man for the position. The Government would be well advised to take that into consideration.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: It is stated in the report which has been made, and which I read to-day as well as yesterday, that these incidents doubtless occurred through ignorance of the officer that the particular form of punishment administered was no longer used in Great Britain. It appeared in the regulations, and on the strength of the regulations they felt entitled to administer that punishment. Further than that, so far as the present case is concerned, and also, apparently, so far as the cases in the West are concerned, there had been very grave breaches of discipline. I do not know as to the particulars of the western cases.
It is not very clear that there were any grave breaches of discipline in the western cases.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I am merely referring to the report, which 3ays that the breach of discipline was flagrant, or something of that kind. From the Provost Marshall's investigation it seemed that aggravated cases only were dealt with in this way. In the Nova Scotia case, a man while under detention escaped, remained away from his regiment for about two weeks and then returned. He had been guilty of six distinct offences within a period of four weeks previous to that. It was, therefore, regarded as a very* aggravated case, and the commanding officer administered this punishment.
\
In the case of an investigation of this kind, is it the officer complained of who investigates and makes the report?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The Provost Marshal made the investigation, not the officer in command. The investigation is made under the direction of the officer commanding the military district.

The Prime Minister has
not so far been good enough to say whether the Government has any intention of going into this question of the fitness of these officers for their positions or the propriety of administering some form of punishment.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Perhaps my
hon. friend did not understand what I said with regard to that. I stated that I would consult the proper officer of the department, who in this case is the Adjutant General. I would ask the opinion also of the Chief of the General Staff, General Gwatkin, who is an officer of long experience and sound judgment, as is, indeed, the Adjutant General himself.

The matter is very far
reaching. In our present condition, when we are attempting to enlist the active service and therefore the sympathy of most of our people in military affairs, such circumstances as these, which are very foreign to our ideas of right and justice, and so very foreign to custom, have a very prejudicial effect. Their tendency would be to prejudice the public mind very greatly against military service. Cases having occurred, it would seem to me that something should be done to demonstrate to the public that such conduct is absolutely contrary to the policy of the country, in military as well as in civil affairs.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
We have not yet the full report of this investigation, but only a summary by wire. It is possible that some recommendations may be made by the officer who is charged with the duty of investigation. My hon. friends will remember what was said by the hon. member for North Simcoe (Mr. Currie) last night, that while 99 per cent, or 999 out of 1,000, may be the very best men you can find, you do occasionally find in a regiment a man who habitually offends against discipline and whose example to the other men in the regiment is very detrimental indeed. Notwithstanding that, instructions 
have been given that this particular form of punishment, which at one time prevailed, but which has now become obsolete in Great Britain, shall not be administered in the future in Canada. I really cannot say anything more about the officers than what I have stated. A consultation will be had with the proper officers of the department, and their view of the conduct of those who are responsible for the administration of punishment on these occasions will be ascertained. Considering that we have- enlisted 320,000 men, who have been trained in Canada during the past eighteen or twenty months, there have been very few instances of anything like this. At the moment I cannot recall anything other than the few cases in the West and a case in Nova Scotia. So in that respect I think, perhaps, we are entitled to congratulate ourselves that so few incidents of a regrettable character have occurred.

While it is true that there may be 99 per cent of the men good and 1 per cent bad, it is also possible that there may be a certain percentage of our officers who are not the highest type of officers. As to this punishment being set out in the field regulations, I do not think there are many officers who would hide behind that. I have no doubt that the same field regulations say that if a man deserts he should be shot. If you are going to say that you should go by the letter of the bond, it would be as much a justification for shooting boys who desert-and some of them, nice boys, do desert-and it w'ould be preposterous to say that the field regulations were in force to that extent, I should think that the very woTd " field " regulations would be enough to convince any man that, in a city like Moosejaw, it is not necessary to adopt such regulations as you would at the salient at Ypres. I should think that the field regulations were made for the firing line. No mention is made in the report, of the young man named O'Brien. I know that the Prime Minister has only a telegraphic report at present and it may be that this case may have been overlooked in the telegram. I see by the press that a meeting of the (battalion, or something of that kind, was held, and a vote was taken to the effect that they would stay by the Colonel, which to my mind is not a good sign. You will always get men who will vote for their colonel, especially that kind of a colonel. There are not many who would desire to have a taste of the cast-iron wheel to. which the men were

tied, and naturally they would think that, all things considered, they had hetteT vote for the colonel as long as he was colonel. The commanding officer, whose name I have never mentioned, may be an honourable officer. He said in a public address in the city of Moosejaw that he has been stabbed from behind. I am not going to enter into any controversy with him, but I will say that I am more convinced now than I was when I first mentioned it that I was discharging my duty when I brought this matter to the attention of the House, and I have no reason to doubt that the address he is reported to have made in Moosejaw last Sunday night referred to my remarks. It was not an utterance an officer should have made. I have my duty to perform, and he has his. So far as I have had any personal relations with him, they have been of unalloyed friendship. I know him very slightly, because he is a stranger in our city. When will the-full report likely be received in Ottawa?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
We expect it
some time in the early part of next week.
Mr. CfLIVER: Last night the Prime Minister referred to an investigation in regard to the Ross rifle. Is that report available?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: ' I think the report could not be brought down; it is of a confidential character.

Was it a British or a

On April
26 some questions were answered with reference to the employment of Mr. J. A. Spidal as Tecruiting officer in the county of Kings. The answer was that he had been in the employ of the department from November 9, 1915, until January 4, 1916. My information is that he is at present at Berwick in command of a detachment of the 219th Battalion, and it is said that he is still in the employ of the Government and is receiving military pay. I am also informed that he has been wearing his uniform and, having been nominated as the Conservative candidate for the legislature, he has recently been attending Conservative meetings in his uniform. It would appear that perhaps there is a misapprehension somewhere. I desire to know if the statement is correct that he has not
been in the employ of this Government since January 4, 1916, and if he has been disporting himself in a military uniform while not in discharge of any duties as an officer?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I have no personal knowledge of the matter. The answer given was communicated in the usual way by the officers of the department. The deputy minister will take a note of the question and give the information later. So-far as concerns the question of engaging in political activities, I do not understand the rule <jf the department or of the War Office to debar a man from becoming a cana candidate.

I did not
say that.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The other day
I had an application from the Premier of Quebec asking for leave of absence for an officer who is on active service. The request was that he should receive leave-of absence for 30 days in order that he might attend to his duties as a candidate in the general elections pending in the province of Quebec. We at once gave him leave of absence for that purpose, and he was relieved of his military duties in order that he might attend to matters requiring his attention as a candidate. The same rule will be observed in regard to all persons on active service, whatever their political affiliations may be.

No objection is taken to his being a candidate, or to his taking a part in politics. He has a perfect right to do so if he so desires. The reason I mentioned the matter was because of an answer to a question on 26th April, to be found on page 3219 of Hansard. The question was: "Is it the intention of the Government to continue to employ Mr. Spiddel in such service?" The answer was, "No." A previous question was: "When was he appointed?" The answer was: "November 9, 1915." Another question was: "What rank does he hold, and what pay does he receive?" The answer was: "No militia rank. $3 per diem from November 9, 1915, to January 4, 1916." ' The inference is that on January 4, 1916, he ceased to hold his position as recruiting officer. In respect to his rank, I am told that he has taken a lieutenant's course at the Royal School of Infantry at Halifax, and that that answer is not correct. It may well be that the other answers were incorrectly given, not intentionally, of course, but through

some misapprehension. It is alleged that this man is now in Berwick in command of a detachment of the 209th Battalion. It is also stated that he still continues in the capacity of recruiting officer, and is drawing pay as such. In support of that statement, the evidence is that he has been going through the country in his uniform, and that he attended a meeting at Kent* ville and was chairman on that occasion. That, however, is only mentioned in passing. I shall be very glad if the minister would get this information, and furnish it as soon as convenient.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I will have inquiry made, and give the information to my hon. friend when the Bill is in committee.

I noticed that the acting minister stated that it was not his intention, and that it had not been the intention of the Minister of Militia, to allow political influence to be used in connection with the department. We all know perfectly well that there has been politics in the Militia Department, and in connection with the army, from the beginning of the war until the present moment; we see it manifested all over the country. I do not say that it would be possible for the Government to do away with it altogether, but there i3 no use in shutting our eyes to the fact that politics cut a very large figure in connection with the running of the Militia Department.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: In what respect?

Let me give my right hon. friend an instance. A battalion is being organized in Prince Albert, and an hon. member of this House is the lieutenant-colonel, while his son-in-law is second in command, having been put over the head of a man who had had military experience. If that is not politics, I do not know what it is. But what I got up to bring to the attention of the acting minister was this: A man named Frank Carew, whose father is a member of the local Legislature, is the paymaster for some soldiers located in Lindsay, Ont. He has clerks to do his work, and, while dressed in military uniform, runs his father's office. He is paid by the Militia Department. That seems to me to look as if political influence was at work. I have information of another case. A man named Roenik, a German, draws pay as bandmaster, though he is not the bandmaster; he is too old to

attend to his duties or to go overseas, and another man named Heffernan is in reality *the leader of the band and bandmaster. In other words, the man who does not do the wr rk draws the pay for it. It strikes me that that savours a little of political influence, and I do not think that that sort of think should be allowed. In my own constituency one man applied for a position as an officer; he is an officer now. He has had a long experience, having been in the Mounted Police force during the greater part of his life, but he told me that another man had been placed over his nead-a very good man, a lawyer, and a good supporter of the Government, but with no military experience whatever, while the other man had put in 20 years in the Mounted Police, and was an officer in a local corps long before the war started; yet he was passed over. Cases like these are numerous throughout the country, and I think it would be well if my right hon. friend, the acting minister, would, as far as possible, do away with that sort of thing and not have experienced military men turned down. I am not speaking now so much of political influence, but of men with some military experience being turned down for men who have had no experience. I do not think that that is in the interest of the Militia Department, or in the interest of our army when it goes across the water. Certainly it requires some experience to enable a man to be a good officer when he goes to the firing line. These are just a few cases that have been brought to my attention. I have heard of many more, but I cannot mention them because I do not know more about them. You hear every day of this man or that man being passed over for some one else with political pull but without any military qualifications.

I think that in justice to the people of the country the statement of the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Turriff) should not go unchallenged. Take for example the battalion which I know very well: discipline prevents me from mentioning the number. The colonel is a Liberal; the majority of the officers were Conservatives, and there were three applicants for the position. Two of them were Conservatives, but 'everybody pulled for the Liberal. When I say " pulled " I do not mean that there was any improper pulling done. They wanted to see the Liberal get the position for the sake of the service. There is no use in sending broadcast

through this country the idea that the Conservative party is honeycombed with vice of that description, because it is not 'so.

I quite agree with the
hon. member for West Peterborough (Mr. Burnham), that this statement should not be allowed'to go unchallenged. From Vancouver we have sent three battalions to the front. The commanding officers of these battalions are all prominent Liberals, prominent citizens, and excellent officers. One of them, who is now at the front-the Prime Minister knows him very well; I will not mention his name-has earned the D.S.O. and other distinctions./ With regard to the case my hon. friend has spoken of, it is quite correct that the commanding officer had for his second-in-command his brother-in-law; but this was not a case of political influence. He appointed his brother-in-law, not because he was a Liberal, but because he bad a liking for him; it was just a little bit of human nature; and the man is discharging his duties in an excellent manner. No one can complain of that; I would not think of suggesting political influence, or that the officer was appointed because he was a Liberal. The brigade commander is also a prominent Liberal and an excellent officer. I have no objection to him whatever. As long as a man can do his duty to the country I do not care a scrap what his politics are, and as far as the district I represent is concerned, I resent the suggestion that politics count one scrap in appointments to the army. I challenge any member to cite one single instance in which 1 have ever suggested politics in the appointment of officers or in the purchase of supplies in any shape ox form. From the day the war broke out I have taken most emphatically the stand that politics should not enter into this war as regards military appointments. It is unwise And unfair to be continually throwing out to the country that our magnificent army is a matter of political patronage; it is not fair, it is not right, and I resent it.

The hon. gentleman
may resent it; I suppose he has a right to. But let me tell him on my responsibility as a member of this House that military affairs in the province I come from are, if I may use his expression, honeycombed with politics from start to finish, it being purely a matter of political patronage, and I challenge the hon. member or any one else to prove to the contrary. In the county from which I come we have Mr. Douglas, who is president of the Conservative Association for the province of Nova Scotia. He is also one of the local members for the county, and has just as firm a grip on every move in every battalion in Cape Breton as he has in what may be regarded as matters of legitimate patronage.
Did my hon. friend say that Mr. Douglas was president of the Conservative Association in Nova Scotia?

I understood that he
was. '
He is not.
If not, a change must have been made in the last few months. He was president last year.

Mr. A. B. Crosby has
been president since last fall.

Mr. Douglas was the
president, at all events, and he is now either vice-president or honorary president. The hon. member for Annapolis knows well the standing that Mr. Douglas has in the Conservative party. I am making no misstatement at all about his position, and if the Prime Minister, either as Prime Minister or as Acting Minister of Militia, will take, the trouble of getting some independent information as to how matters are managed in the county of Cape Breton, he will find that they are absolutely honeycombed, to again use my hon. friend's expression, with political influence. We are not looking for anything else; we do not expect anything else; we never get anything else. I say to the hon. member for Vancouver and to the Prime Minister that not one man east of Halifax has received any military prominence since the war broke out, unless he was a supporter of the Conservative party and identified with the cause. We have one gentleman in Halifax of whom I am very proud. He bears the name of the Prime Minister, and is a well-recognized Liberal. His ability prominence and personality have brought him forward; they could not keep him back; but he is the only Liberal in Nova Scotia who has received any prominence whatever since the war broke out. I challenge any one to name any other man who 'has come to the front in any way whatsoever in the province of Nova Scotia, unless he was well recognized to be in harmony with the Government of the day.
We are told that there is no political influence in the matter of supplies for the troops. I asked some questions a few days

ago as to supplies for the 94th at Sydney Mines and North Sydney, and I got the answer that the officers went around and got bids from different parties for the supplies. I have the names of those who furnished the supplies, and I should be glad to show them to the Prime Minister; he knows some of them. There is not a man on the list but got his name down, through political influence, either directly or indirectly; there is not a prominent Liberal on the list at all, and the men who supplied the goods got their money direct from the department without there being any competition. We are not complaining of that; we are not looking for anything else. The acting minister-perhaps not he, for he has not said very much about it, but the Minister of Militia-used to say boastfully that there was no suc'h thing. If he had kept quiet about it we would say nothing, but we cannot listen to such boastful declarations when the truth is absolutely to the contrary. We do not expect any patronage' to come to us in Nova Scotia in public works or railway matters, or anything of that kind, so long as we are in opposition; and that is precisely the policy that has been followed in Nova Scotia in regard to military matters as well. It is the absolute truth that only by some unavoidable accident has anything fallen to the lot of a Liberal. On the other hand, the Liberals have joined the ranks and are doing their part just as well as the others; men and women, Liberal and Conservative, are connected with every patriotic society, doing what they can; but when it comes to preferment or an appointment to a military position the line is strictly drawn; there is no communication between the Jews and Samaritans in things of that kind. We do not complain, but we want hon. gentlemen to keep quiet, and not make vain and improper and unsupported boasts about these things.
Does my hon. friend say my remarks were improper?

I am referring to no province but my own. Whatever my sins may be, I keep to facts within my own knowledge. But if I were to judge by general politics, I should say that Vancouver is about as corrupt as they make them.
I challenge my hon. friend to prove that.

On general grounds, I prefer to take the declaration of so distinguished a Conservative as Sir Charles Hibbert Tupper,. who says that 4 p.m. the Conservative party in that province is steeped to the lips in corruption. I leave the issue between that distinguished member of the Conservative party and my hon. friend. I do not wish to find fault, especially as the Prime Minister is head of the department for the present, and is perhaps not so familiar with the details as the real head might be. I was in the province of Nova Scotia a few days ago when some complaints were brought to my notice and I wish, in the kindliest way, to bring them to the notice of the Prime Minister. I have reference to the 195th Battalion, which is now in camp at Broughton, a small place in a remote part of the county of Cape Breton. I do not quite understand why they were sent there. It is not a convenient place for a railway; there is no proper sewerage; there is no water system at the place, and it is practically in the woods where the land is not even cleared and the tents, I am told, are in amongst stumps and 'stones and uncultivated land. The men are complaining that they are not properly looked after and that they are not well fed. I was also told by my Roman Catholic friends that although the soldiers are there for several weeks, over several Sundays, no provision at all has been made for any Roman Catholic services. As they are complaining about these things, I bring them to the notice of the minister in the best manner that I can and with as little publicity as possible, and I trust that these men shall be properly taken care of and housed and well fed, and that their spiritual wants will be looked after as they ought to be.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Just a word or two with regard to what some of my hon. friends have said. There seems to have . been an impression that the Minister of Militia spends his time making appointments amongst the force of almost 140,000 now under training in Canada. The appointments as I understand, aTe recommended by the Officer Commanding, and the Minister of Militia very often does not even know the names of the officers who are recommended. He takes the view of the officer on the spot as to those whom he should recommend, and he does not concern himself more about the matter, because it would be impossible for him to make personal inquiry into the officers who are selected by the commanding officers

of the different battalions to fill the various positions.

Who authorizes each battalion and selects the commanding officer?
Sir ROBERT BORDEN- That is done from headquarters.	*
By the Minister of Militia?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I presume the minister acts upon his own judgment and takes the report of the proper officers of his department as to the competency of the selection which is presented for his approval. My hon. friend (Mr. McKenzie) has referred to some matters in the province of Nova S-cotia. I do not know very much about the details, but I am informed that the son of the hon. member for Pictou has been appointed as the adjutant of one of the battalions there. I am also informed that Mr. Rolston, who was the opponent, I think, of the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Rhodes) at the last election, has been very rapidly promoted, and that Col. Parsons, who was appointed to be second in command of the 185th Battalion, is a very strong Liberal. The remarks of the hon. member for North Cape Breton and Victoria are rather surprising in view of the fact that not long since a resolution was passed, I think, at a Liberal convention in Nova Scotia, giving the crbdit for the organization of the Highland Brigade in Nova Scotia to the Hon. Mr. Murray, premier of that province. If Mr. Murray has imbued himself with the political aspect of the situation to the extent which my hon. friend suggests, I admit that my hon. friend's remarks which must be taken as an animadversion upon him, are well founded, but I do not believe that Mr. Murray's connection with such matters has had anything more to do with politics than the connection of the Minister' of Militia. It is a fact as reported to me that great credit is taken by the Liberal party in Nova Scotia for the organization of the Highland Brigade. Yet my hon. friend stands on the floor of this Parliament and says that the whole thing is honeycombed with politics. If you put those two observations together, you have a result which is not flattering to .the patriotic attitude of hon. gentlemen on the other side.
The battalion at Broughton is under the command of an officer whom I do not personally know except that I saw him in Nova Scotia last autumn, but I have the best possible report as to Col. Day. He
is, I am told, a very able man, a very patriotic man and a man who, I believe, would be inspired by no other consideration or feeling than the desire to do his duty. I have not the slightest idea as to what his politics are, nor have I ever inquired. I would like to say that if the province of Nova Scotia has been honeycombed, as my hon. friend suggests, by partisan considerations, in connection with military affairs, it is different, I believe, from every other province in Canada, because I know that in other provinces gentlemen who are associated with the Liberal party have been promoted to the very highest commands. That is true in the province of Ontario, and many illustrations could be given. As a matter of fact, I venture to think that for every complaint made with regard to some gentleman having been passed over because he happened to be a Liberal, I could give two complaints from Conservatives who thought they were passed over in order that Liberals might be appointed in their stead. In the province of New Brunswick we appointed a member of this House, Col. McLean, to a very important command. He was at Valcartier last autumn, and he has been rendering very good service. In the province of Ontario the highest commands are in many instances given to gentlemen who have a very high standing in the ranks of the Liberal party, and I desire to affirm to -this committee my most sincere belief that from the first of this war up to the present time, the Minister of Militia and Defence has never in a single instance been actuated by any political consideration in any appointment that he has made. That is my sincere belief, from what I have seen and known of his conduct during this war. With regard to the appointment of a Catholic chaplain to the 185th Battalion, I understand that Father Gillis has been appointed.

The Prime Minister says that there are no politics in the department, and that the minister is guided in his appointments by the recommendations of the officer in charge. I would like to call to the attention of the Prime Minister that Toryism gets in its work in making the recommendations to the officer in charge. The Tory politician in my county is supreme so far as military matters are concerned, and he says to the officers: If you do not do my bidding, off goes your head. I will point out to the Prime Minister-and he can look up the record-three

men who were rather independent. Col. McRae, of the 94th Battalion, would not play^ second fiddle to John C. Douglas. Off went his head; he was discharged. Major Gillis, an independent officer and a good Scotchman, would see John C. Douglas in Jericho before he would be pulled around by the nose by him, and off went his head. Major McLean, who was in charge of the 94th Battalion at North Sydney, was known to be a Liberal. He would not be dictated to by John C. Douglas and his minions, and off went his head.
Who is John C. Douglas?

He is the Tory manager in the county of Cape Breton. The men who are in charge and who are human enough to think that it is nice to stay in office, do precisely what John C. Douglas tells them to do, and through the medium of those men the Tory appointments come to the minister, and he can flap his holy wings and say: I know nothing about the matter; it is done absolutely without any bias at all. But he knows that nothing can come to him but what is absolutely lined with Toryism.

I cannot allow the remarks of my hon. friend (Mr. McKenzie) to go unchallenged. It has been whispered and insinuated many times regarding British Columbia. The leader of the Opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) laughed with considerable glee when the hon. member for North Cape Breton (Mr. McKenzie) made the Temark. But I challenge the Tight hon. gentleman and the hon. member for North Cape Breton to cite a single sentence falling from the lips of Sir Charles Hibbert Tupper in which he cast any reflection whatever upon a single act of the Administration at Ottawa or upon a single act of mine as the representative of Vancouver in this House.
I shall be glad to do so if he will give me the time.
Do so. I will take my seat to give the hon. gentleman his opportunity.
I have not the papers before me, but on Monday-

Sir Charles Hibbert Tupper did consider it his duty to take the platform against the Provincial Government. With that I have nothing to do, and this House has nothing to do; the people of British Columbia will judge of that. But by not one single word has Sir

Charles Hibbert Tupper cast any aspersion, direct or indirect, upon this Government or upon any administrative act of this Government. And I want to say something further for the consolation of my hon. friend the leader of the Opposition and the hon. member for North Cape Breton, and that is that the only corruption that has come to light in the last election is the wholesale plugging on behalf of Mr. M. A. Macdonald, the Liberal hero in Vancouver. They brought men by the score from Seattle, self-confessed pluggers, and voted them for Mr. Macdonald, the Grit candidate. That is the only corruption that has been shown in the city of Vancouver in connection with the recent election.
Will the hon. gentleman inform the House what this House has to do with that?

An aspersion has been
cast upon the province of British Columbia by the hon. member for North Cape Breton, and even at the risk of being out of order I would resent it on the floor of this House; and I think I have a right to do so when these statements are made here. For months and months the papers of eastern Canada have been circulating false and slanderous stories regarding British Columbia, and it is about time some one said a word to the people bf the East in regard to my province. If time permitted, I could convince any reasonable member of this House that conditions in British Columbia, politically and otherwise, are a credit to the province and to Canada as a whole. Unless an hon. member is prepared to bring some specific charge or statement before the House, he should respect the representatives of the people from that province.

I had the pleasure of
visiting Halifax, last fall, and while there I called upon several of the prominent mercantile establishments. I was told by a reputable firm that when ships of the imperial navy came into port at Halifax, tenders were publicly asked for supplies for the ships, but when supplies were needed for a Canadian ship, a few people were selected to tender. In my opinion, this way of buying supplies should cease; in this matter, we ought to attain as high a standard as the Imperial authorities. The firm that gave me this information is a reputable firm, and I think its testimony is conclusive evidence that, to some extent at any rate, there is a disposition to carry

on the abominable practice of petty politics and party patronage in the purchase of war supplies.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
That relates to
the Department of the Naval Service, and so I cannot pretend to be familiar with the matter; but I should be surprised to learn that the statement of my hon. friend has any foundation whatever. If the supplies for British ships are purchased through the Department of the -Naval Service it is inconceivable that they should have one system for British ships and another system for Canadian ships. To what Canadian ships does the hon. member refer?

I refer to ships under the authority of the Canadian Naval Department, but the ships to which I refer as publicly asking for tenders are under the authority of the Imperial Government. They are, as I understand it, patrolling out of New York and defending the route to the British Islands.
