Their supplies are purchased in a different way from those required by ships under control of the Canadian Government,

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: So far as transports are concerned-and I do not know whether the hon. gentleman has reference to transports or not-everything.is managed by a gentleman who was formerly associated with the Canadian Pacific Railway, Mr. A. H. Harris, who has been acting as overseas director of transport. And, if I am not very much mistaken, the firm employed as ships' agent for the transports, is a strong Liberal firm. As to the small patrol ships, I do not know how they are supplied, but the Minister of the Naval Service will know ana I will direct his attention to the observations of my hon. friend.

I have never troubled the House very much with mention of politics in the administration of public affairs, and shall not do so now; but, as the question has been raised concerning influence in military appointments, I may take the opportunity to read from the Edmonton Journal, a Conservative newspaper, something which may throw some light on the matter. This is from the Journal of the 6th of March, 1916:
Major Allan Elliott Declines Offer to Command Guard-Will Remain with the 51st Bat-tallion Which is Soon to he Moved to the Front.
As predicted by the Journal on Saturday, the appointment as officer commanding the 218th
Irish Guards was tendered Major Allan Elliott of the 51st Battalion, by a deputation consisting of A. F. Ewing, M.L.A., Alderman R. N. Frith, and Percy Abbott. The Advisory Committee of representative Irish citizens which is working in unison with IA ,-Colom l McKenery in furthering the interests of the Irish Guards had unanimously decided upon Major Elliott as a fitting soldier to take over this command.
You will observe, Mr. Chairman, that the Irish citizens had decided that Major Elliott was a suitable person to be colonel of a regiment, but that it was a committee . consisting of Mr. Ewing, the Conservative M.L.A., Alderman R. N. Frith, ex-president of the Conservative Association, and Mr. Percy Abbott, who is very prominent in Conservative circles-I do not know what particular office he holds at the present time-these three gentlemen who, as stated by this newspaper supporter of hon. gentlemen opposite, went to Major Elliott and absolutely tendered to him the command, and it was to them he refused to accept it. I think it is only fair, in view of the discussions that have taken place, to lay the facts before the House.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Where a regiment is proposed to be raised from a particular nationality, I think it is very often desired to obtain the views of those who are very likely to be members of the battalion, and to learn whether or not they have confidence in the particular officer who is proposed to be selected. Something of that kind was done in this case; some representative gentlemen were asked to consult Mr. Elliott on the subject, as he was connected with another battalion, and to ascertain whether or not, if the appointment were offered to him, he would accept it.
Mr. MeKENZIE:	The member for Vancouver (Mr. Stevens) challenged me to produce proof of certain statements which I made. To take up the challenge of my hon. friend would not, perhaps, be exactly in line with the resolution before us; but I do not want to be charged with making observations that are not backed up by the facts. What I am about to read has reference particularly to Mr. Bowser, and brings in Sir Richard McBride. If I know anything about the politics of British Columbia, that has been the whole push for the last eighteen years-iBowser and McBride, McBride and Bowser. I venture to say the hon. member for Vancouver could never have got the nomination for Vancouver if it had not been for the sup-

port of Bowser and McBride and McBride [DOT]and Bowser.
My hon. friend is making a very grave mistake.

My hon. friend may
say so, now that Mr. McBride is out of the country, but I venture to say that when he was in his palmy days no one from British Columbia could say or do anything except by his authority.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman
has, I think, sufficiently verified his assertion of a moment ago, and I do not know that any useful purpose can be served by -this discussion. I submit to the committee that the Chairman is placed in a somewhat helpless position from day to day inasmuch as ministers announce that the widest possible discussion may be had upon a given resolution, notwithstanding the fact that the rules state explicitly that the discussion must be strictly relevant to the item under consideration. Of course, there is nothing for the Chairman to do but submit to the wishes of the committee in that respect, but the committee could assist the Chairman by keeping within such wide bounds as are laid down for discussion in committee. I sincerely hope that the hon. [DOT]member will not pursue the subject any further.

If I may be allowed
to finish what I want to say, I will not add anything to my Temarks. The hon. member for Vancouver put me in the position That I was making statements for which I had no authority; I am simply going to read my authority.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member will [DOT]see that this will involve a reply from the hon. member for Vancouver and so on, ad infinitum.
Permit me to say this: I have the telegram of Sir Charles Tupper in my hand which denounces in the worst terms the Tory party-and you will not permit me to read it.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member will have ample opportunity before the session is over. I think he himself will agree with me that it will be far wiser not to pursue the subject any further.

Something has been said
to-day about a surplus of officers in Canada and something was said on a previous occasion about a surplus of officers in Eng-lland. What is the position in England

with regard to what may be called supernumerary officers? The statement was made here that as battalions have gone overseas, for one reason or another officers have ceased to be attached to them and are maintained on pay in England without rendering service. If that occurs to any large degree it is an evil that should not be permitted. It burdens the country and is a discrimination in favour of men who do not merit it. I certainly think the committee is entitled to understand from the head of the department what that situation is.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: There is a supply of officers in Great Britain, above what is called the establishment. A communication was sent within the past two weeks to General Carson for information on the subject and the reply was to the effect that every one'of the officers was attached to some unit and that every one of them was being employed. A fuller statement will come by letter. Pending the receipt of this reply a further inquiry was addressed to General Carson, to which a reply has not yet been received, so far as I am aware.

I wish to bring to the at* tention of the minister a certain'instance that I have already discussed in part with the Minister of the Interior, who advised me that I should take the matter up with the Department of Militia. It relates to a battalion which was raised at Edmonton, and which was listed at Valcartier as the 9th Battalion. When war broke out there was in Edmonton a volunteer battalion known as the 101st. It was at full strength and was under the command of one Colonel Osborne. When war wa3 declared this battalion offered its services as a body to the Government for service overseas; at least that is my information. It was not accepted, but authority was given foT the raising of an overseas battalion, with the result that a battalion was raised immediately for -overseas service under Colonel Osborne, and that battalion was amongst the first, if not the first, to reach Valcartier, although it came from Edmonton, further away than almost any other battalion that came to Valcartier. It came to Valcartier over strength; I think there were some 1,300 men in the battalion. Some little time after it had been at Valcartier I am informed that as Colonel Osborne sat in his tent one morning another gentleman, Colonel Maynard Rogers, entered the tent and said to Colonel Osborne:

.154a
" I am in command of the 9th Battalion." Colonel Maynard Rogers is a former resident of Ottawa. He removed to Edmonton and was finally appointed the superintendent of Jasper Park. Having had military experience, when war broke out he volunteered his services, and they were accepted. He left his employment at Jasper Park, came to Valcartier, and was given command of the 9th Battalion, over the head of the man who had raised it and had brought it down there, and with just the amount of ceremony, so I am informed, that I have related to the committee. Colonel Osborne accepted the situation and continued with the battalion as second in command. The battalion went overseas in due course, reached England, and while it was in England-I do not know all of what occurred, but in the end Colonel Osborne was retired altogether from the battalion, and, though retaining his rank, I suppose, was returned to Canada without military employment. My information is that it was found that Colonel Rogers was not competent for the position of colonel in the field; the fact was, at any rate, that the battalion was broken up and there was not any 9th Battalion from that time forward. The members of that battalion were distributed around among other battalions, and when I read the casualty lists issued in pamphlet or book form some time ago, I noticed that in the lists of casualties in the various battalions were men " formerly 9th Battalion." My information was that Colonel Rogers never went on active service in Europe, that he was one of the unattached officers in England until General Lessard was sent over to England; and then this Colonel Rogers was given a position as staff officer to him, and I suppose has been engaged in that service since. But from the time that the battalion went to England until he went to the front with General Lessard, so far as I am aware, he did no military service, and my opinion is that not only did he do no military service but, by reason of his lack of military ability, he did a serious dis-service in having been the cause of breaking up the 9th Battalion. At the same time, as the Minister of the Interior informs us, Colonel Rogers is drawing his salary as superintendent of Jasper park, $2,400 a year. He has been, of course, drawing his salary as Lieut.-Colonel during all this time. But not only is he not rendering the country or the Empire any service, but he rendered ,a serious dis-service by reason of his having 224
been put in a position which he was not competent to fill. I do not know how many other cases there may be like that, but it appears to me that when there i3 such a startling case it should be made public, and I hope there are no other such cases. But the information that has come to me is that there are a very large number of them. The Minister of the Interior told us that Colonel Rogers drew his salary as superintendent of Jasper park, and was still drawing it. I say that is wrong. When it was found that this gentleman was not adapted for the command of a military battalion for active service, he should, in all common sense, have been returned to civil employment, for which I believe he was entirely fitted. Remember that I have no fault to find with Colonel Rogers personally or in his civil employment, but, having left his civil employment and undertaken military employment, and being found unfit for it, the results being as they were-and they were certainly very displeasing to men who are interested and to many of their friends -I cannot give the administration under which such a condition exists, that commendation that I should be very glad to give, and certainly such a state of affairs does not tend to efficiency or satisfaction.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I am rather surprised at my hon. friend's animadversions on Colonel Rogers; unless he has good grounds for them. Colonel Rogers has had a long military experience in the militia of Canada, to my certain knowledge; and unless I am mistaken he also saw active service in the South African war.
He did.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I understand he is engaged in Great Britain in connection with the training of the troops there'. I do not know all the particulars. So far as Colonel Osborne is concerned, I do not remember ever hearing of him or of the incident to which my hon. friend refers. That occurred a long time ago. If the Minister of Militia were here doubtless he could give some information. I shall have inquiry made. If my hon. friend has anything else as to which he would like information, I wish he would state it now so that we can take it up at the proper time.
Who was the contractor for supplying clothing to the department last year, and who is the contractor at the present time?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I really could not say. We will get the information and give it to my hon. friend.

There is another matter to which I wish to draw attention and it is in regard to recruiting. The Prime Minister said the other day that in the scheme of recruiting an effort was made to direct the exertions of those who were concerned to different localities where they would Tesult in the least disturbance to the economic situation. I am compelled to take the view that that has not been the guiding policy of the department. My opinion is that they have been guided simply and solely by the possibility of securing recruits, and that wherever recruiting was good they took all the recruits they could without regard to the result to the community at large. I have no fault to find with the action of the department, but I do find fault with the assertion that discrimination has been used when there has been no such discrimination. If I may be permitted to giye a statement of the recruiting that has taken place in Northern Alberta, of course with Edmonton as its headquarters, it will be seen just how much and how far consideration was paid to the circumstances which my right hon. friend has dealt with. On August 12, 1914, 120 men were recruited for the Princess Pats; on August 13, 116; and on Aug. 14, 65 men. On Aug. 22, the 101st sent 908 men. On August 26, the 19th Alberta Dragoons sent 206 men. On August 27, the 101st, that is the 9th Battalion, sent 350 men. That made 1,250 men in that 9th Battalion. On the 3rd of November a contingent of 100 men was sent to Quebec City, and in order to let the committee know the exact circumstances of that draft, I may say that a telegram was sent to Edmonton saying that 100 men were wanted. Those men threw down what they were engaged in and left the city, they did not take time to settle their affairs in any way. They simply took the next train for Quebec under the impression that the city had been attacked, or that there was some catastrophe that made such a call for men urgent. When they got to Quebec they found that all they were wanted for was to fill up a regiment that was somewhat short of its full number. On Nov. 16, 101 men went to Calgary to join the 31st Battalion there. On Nov. 17, another detachment went to Calgary to joint the 31st Battalion; on Nov. 25, 110 men went to Calgary

to join the 31et Battalion; on Nov. 28, 40 men enlisted for the Lethbridge Artillery; on Dec. 12, 40 more men went to the 31st at Calgary. On Jan. 4, the Mounted Rifles, recruited under Colonel Kemmis, secured 164 men; on May 7, the first Universities Company sent a draft of 9 men; on May 8, a draft of 250 men was taken for the 51st Battalion, under Captain Hig-ginson; on May 24, the second Universities Company sent 16 men; on May 29, the 49th Battalion, with base company, sailed for overseas, 1,300 strong. On June 1st, "C" Squad, 3rd C.M.R., Major Fane, recruited 164; on June 24, the 3rd Universities Company recruited 35 men; on August 13, another draft of the 51st Battalion, 270 men, went forward; on September 6, a draft of the 63rd Battalion, 252 men, went forward; on September 11, a draft of the 65th Battalion, 250 men, went forward; on October 4, the 4th Universities Company, 20 men, went forward; on November 17, a Pioneer Battalion, 75 men, went forward; on December 3, Serbian and Montenegrin reservists, to the number of 80, went forward; on December 5, the 5th Universities Company, 50 men, went forward; on December 19, the American Legion, 100 men, went forward; on December 20, 99 French-Canadians went east to join a regiment in St. Boniface.
Besides those who have gone forward, there was the 63rd Battalion, with a base company in the city numbering 1,132 men. It transferred to the Pioneers 35 men, and to the 50th Battalion 23 men. There was also the 66th Battalion with a base company, numbering 1,136, and it transferred to the Pioneers 50, and to the Artillery 10 men. In addition there was the 51st Battalion, with a base company, 1,263 men, and it transferred to the Pioneers 35 men and to the Artillery 10. There were also the 138th Battalion, 1,050 men; the 151st Battalion, 1,050 men; the 194th Highlanders (authorized) 1,050 men-this battalion is not up to strength yet-and a battalion to be raised by Lt. Col. Bowen, 1,050 men. There have been two other battalions authorized there since. I think this list will show that the only consideration in recruiting seems to have been to get men if they can be got. There has been no effort to distribute the quota throughout the country according to population; no rule at all other than to get the men if they can be got.
Did some of these men not come from long distances?
Yes, from the northern part of the province.
So that the recruiting covered a very large territorial area?

Yes, the men came from all parts of northern Alberta, Edmonton, of course, being the recruiting centre. But even so, according to the Ottawa Journal, the province of Alberta has already re-'cruited some 2,000 more men, according to population, than would be its fair proportion of the 500,000 caJlled for by the Prime Minister last January, and still the recruiting is going on. I am not objecting to that; we are perfectly satisfied that that should be so. But when it is. asserted that there has been' discrimination used, I want to say that the facts do not bear that contention out.
A further remark which I desire to make is that at the present time there are six battalions recruiting from Northern Alberta with headquarters at Edmonton. I do not consider that it is in the interest of recruiting that there should be so many battalions recruiting at the same time. When two battalions are recruiting at the same time, there may possibly be an element of competition that is good, but when there is a larger number of battalions, all looking for men, it does not tend to secure the best results. I do not think that the department is well advised in having so many battalions recruiting at once. When an authorization is made, and two battalions are recruited up to full strength, let two more be authorized, if that is thought desirable, but to authorize four or five different battalions to recruit at the same time, in a small place and in a thinly populated country, makes the work of the officers who are attending to the recruiting very difficult, much more difficult than if they were permitted to recruit, say, only two battalions at a time. I see the acting minister is not in the House at the present moment, but I would like to hear from him.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: We have sent for him.

The item can
stand.
Civil Government-Department of Trade and Commerce-to provide for 16 clerkships in the third division, subdivision " B," Census and Statistics Branch, at $600 each, $9,600.

This item looks as if it involved a large addition to the
224J
service, but in reality there is no addition. It simply means that we are putting on the permanent list clerks Who, since 1911, have been on the temporary list. These temporary clerks constitute quite a large proportion of the help in the Census and Statistics Department because of the change in character of the work. When compilation ceases these clerks are laid off, and when compilation is at its height the number of clerks is at its maximum. After compilation in connection with the last census ceased the term of service of these temporary clerks came to an end. Amongst them were sixteen of the very best clerks who had become adepts in the working of the different machines and in the peculiar kinde of compilation that are made and what we wish to do now is to put them on the permanent list, so that these experienced and really good hands may be kept in the Census Department for the regular work. Their services will become necessary soon, if not immediately, in connection with the compilation of the Northwest Census, which is to be taken in June. After that there will be sufficient work of a steady and permanent kind to employ them. We do not want to have them dispersed after they have been trained for three or four years, and, when we come to need assistance, be compelled to get fresh hands and train them.
I understand that these clerks are to be paid at 1600 a year?
They are put on at the salary which they are getting at the present time, which is $600, and they will go up to $900.
By regular progression?

By the regular gradation.
To provide for the development and extension of Canadian trade, $150,000.
What is the programme?

This is an item which the committee is asked to vote in relation to the programme which I outlined in the House some two weeks ago. A portion of this amount will be used for the extension of trade commissionerships, as they may be required. There is a vote in the main Estimates which is insufficient to accomplish the work which will be neces-

sary during the year 1917, and a portion of this vote will be used for that purpose, but just what portion I do not know; it will depend upon what circumstances demand, and somewhat upon how the war progresses. I think I explained before that we are opening new trade commissioner-ships in Russia-one at Petrograd, and one at Omsk, in Siberia, with some sub-trade commissionerships in cities tributary to these two centres. These are not very important, however, as the salaries paid to the men are not ldrge, they being correspondents and not regular trade commissioners. Then, we are preparing a trade commissioner for Italy, and in the course of the year he will be ready to take his place and engage in the work there. Then, two other sub-commissioners are being trained for work in ether parts, as necessities may develop.
Whereabouts in Italy will the trade commissioner be stationed ?

Of that I am not certain. The trade commission of which I spoke the other day in the House, in the course of its investigations, is to make a short stay in Italy, and we shall be better able to discuss the question of headquarters after we have made some further inquiry, and, possibly, after their return. The trade commissioners will also visit France, Belgium, and the United Kingdom. The commission will consist of six members. It is an honorary commission, but of course their expenses will be paid. There are also to be attached to the commission, for working purposes, a number of representatives of large special interests. These representatives or experts accompany the commissioners in an honorary and unpaid capacity, the interests themselves providing the men. A certain amount of expenses will of course be incurred in connection with this commission, and they will be paid out of the $150,000.
I stated also that it was the intention to form a bureau of commercial information. That will have to be organized, and will take a certain amount of money. It is not the intention of the department to rush into a full-blown bureau of commercial information, but rather to proceed by judicious steps from a small beginning to a greater enlargement afterwards. But a considerable amount of expense will be necessary even to make a small beginning. I am not able

to tell the committee just how 5 p.m. much will be expended, nor the exact plans on which the work will proceed, although I have the plans fairly well mapped out- A little more consideration, and the advice of experienced men, together with a study of the mode of operating that is followed in other countries, will no doubt have an influence upon the establishment and methods to be pursued. Those who have followed the course of matters incidental to trade and commerce in Great Britain will know that the British Government made a very elaborate selection of articles of German and Austrian production, and collected a very large and representative exhibit. They have been showing that exhibit in the large cities of the United Kingdom for the last eight or nine months. I got into early communication with the Board of Trade in England and have been successful in getting their consent to having the exhibit put into the hands of the Department of Trade and Commerce for Canada. It will be brought out and exhibited in a number of our large cities, and at the Canadian National Exhibition in Toronto, which is held in the latter part of August and the early part of September. In order to exhibit that properly some expenditure will be necessary, and all the expenses in connection with it, from the time it leaves London until it returns there, will of course be borne by Canada, and disbursed by my own department. The object of the exhibit is to show manufacturers and producers in Great Britain and in Canada, as it will be exhibited here, the kind of articles, the quality of the articles, and the cost of the articles which were so largely supplied by German and Austrian producers to Great Britain, and largely also to Canada and all the other overseas Dominions. That exhibit, will come under this vote. The necessity for research work along various lines of production and industry is, I think, perfectly understood and appreciated in Canada. Whilst a good deal has been done in that respect, Canada has suffered as most other countries have, from not having had an eye out in that direction long ago and not having adapted means for linking together more closely than has been done hitherto the laboratory and the research chamber with the practical working out of industrial and productive operations. So it was that the Germans, having given great attention to that, having laid great stress upon it and having understood its necessity in the industrial trade competition, had arrogated

and gathered to themselves in the years before the war a monopoly of many of the most important processes connected with industrial production. When the war broke out and the connection was changed, Great Britain herself, as almost every other nation, woke up to the fact that invaluable sources and necessities for supplies were monopolized by the country which was now her enemy, and the British manufacturers were left, so to speak, high and dry. The best exemplification of that is what happened in reference to dyestuffs and chemical products connected with textile work. The entire world outside of Germany was thrown into utter and absolute confusion because of the fact that, in the course of the preceding years, a monopoly of that kind of product had gradually been gained by Germany, and when the war broke out, it was almost a complete monopoly. Then again, everyone knows, if they look into and think about the matter, that we probably waste enough in Canada every year to make a very large contribution to the wealth of the country; we waste in many way things which are useful, simply throwing them into the waste heap. What we want is to get concentrated upon all those points the research power of the country, to get it organized, to have it, as it were, mobilized, and to get our attention fixed upon the utilization of waste products which are of inestimable value when chemical and scientific research finds out their qualities and their adaptations, and is able to put them within the power of productive enterprise, so that they become utilized by our manufacturers and confer great wealth and advantage upon the country. In all parts of this country there are more or less of these research resources. Our universities are in part equipped for them-some of them very well equipped; chemical societies and associations are doing their part of .the work; individual chemists are at work, and I have in view the idea of linking up to a certain extent with the Bureau of Information these sources of research, having them co-ordinated so that they shall not be overlapping, having some directive power given to them so that when these questions come up, they may undergo the analysis of a competent directive body or committee that shall apportion these different items of research to the university or the laboratory which is best fitted for them. The universities are strongly disposed to enter into a co-operative effort in that respect. We have been in consultation for the last year more or less, and I
think it is possible to work out a not very expensive plan by which research work in connection with the different universities of this country, the Chemical Association of Canada, and other laboratory or individual research sources, may be undertaken in such a way that it will enure very much to the benefit of Canada from an industrial point of vieV. Manufacturers' associations in this country are very much in favour of that co-operative work, and I hope to be able with a part of this vote to assist in that object. Those are the points with reference to which the vote will chiefly be used.

I would like to add a word or two to what the minister has said, and I appreciate the points that he has raised. With regard to the dye question, if the minister could in any way hurry up the matter, I am sure it would be in the interest of the commercial life of Canada. I know that if to-day you endeavour to place an order in the textile trade, the trade will ask you, say on an order for cheap flannel, for ten cents per yard extra if it is to be died navy blue; the Dominion Textile 'Company will tell you that they cannot give you navy blue prints at all, so that it is very important in the interest of the future of Canada that we should be able to provide those dyes within this Empire, and in Canada if that be possible. It may be that the consumption in Canada is not sufficiently large for us to engage in the manufacture of those special dyes, but we may be able to receive them from the United Kingdom or from the United States. We should, however, encourage the manufacture in Canada of those chemical dyes that are required by our textile manufacturers, and I heartily congratulate the minister on the undertaking that he has brought before us.

I think my hon. friend has opened up a very wide field and one which will prove of very great advantage, but there is something which is as important, if not more important, in regard to everything he has stated just now, and that is technical education. What my hon. friend undertakes to do will certainly produce very good results, but he will find himself balked at almost every step by the want of technical knowledge amongst the population. The Germans have undoubtedly been ahead of every other nation in the application of chemistry to industry; that seems to have been their specialty; in that they have excelled even the Americans, who are supposed to be

'the most inventive of all nations. I think the chemical manufacture of dyes was invented by a Frenchman, but it is now exclusively the property of the Germans, and they have applied it to industry in a manner which has not been approached, much less excelled, by any other nation. It has been largely due to their system of technical education. It seems to me that if my hon. friend would supplement what he has done by some scheme of technical education, he would do a great deal toward what he has in mind. I am afraid my hon. friend will have a long time to wait before we have these things in Canada. They are the result of the spread of knowledge, and in that respect we can learn a useful lesson from Germany.

Has the hon. minister
anything to tell us as to the personnel of this commission?

I am not able
to give the names to-day. I have selected the men, and their names, I suppose, are now before the Governor General, but it is not possible to give those names until the Order in Council has been passed. On Monday, however, I shall be able to give the names.
Compassionate allowance to the widow of the late James Barr, deputy grain inspector, who was killed while in the performance of his duties at Canadian Pacific elevator " D," Fort William, Ontario, $1,000.

This was a particularly hard case. Mr. Barr was for a long time in the employ of the Government as Deputy Grain Inspector. He lost his life by falling and being sucked into the elevator. He leaves a widow and three small children. The usual-or what seems to be the usual-gratuity of $1,000 is recommended here.

The Minister of Trade and Commerce told us that on any item of his Estimates we might bring up any subject relating to his department. As this is the last item in these Supplementary Estimates, I desire to ask a question relating to the steamer service between the mainland and tne Magdalen islands. A letter that I have received from an old friend in the Magdalen islands, the collector of customs, informs me that the Lady Sybil, a steamer built some years ago expressly for the route between Pictou, Prince Edward Island and Magdalen islands, had been sold. I do not know whether she has

been sold to the Admiralty or to some private firm. She rendered excellent service on this route. The statement is made that she is to be replaced by the Amelia. This the people of the Magdalen Islands can hardly believe. Fifteen years ago the Amelia was on the route and was classed as a very inferior steamer. The steamer was partly wrecked, and a number of those on board perished, amongst them the owner himself, Mr. Leslie, formerly member of the local Legislature for the Magdalen Islands. The steamer was afterwards completely discarded; and now we are told that this old steamer is to replace the Lady Sybil which w.as certainly a credit to the department and to the service. I would urge upon the minister, before signing any contract-or, if the contract is signed before paying any subsidy-to have a proper inspection of the vessel. The route is a rough one, as the hon. minister, who comes from the Maritime Provinces, knows, and it will be dangerous for people to travel on that steamer unless repairs have been made which make her practically a new steamer.

The Lady Sybil was bought out from the service. I do not know who bought her or where she went. I imagine she commanded a good price and that her owner-^and operator for a number of years-came to the conclusion that he could not have a better time than this to dispose of his property. Last year we only kept her by great persuasion as the owner wished to sell her then. But this year no persuasion could persuade, and she is gone. The difficulty was to get any vessel for the route, and for a time I thought we should have to borrow from the Marine and Fisheries the Princess-
She is a good steamer.

However, the
Amelia, though out of sight, has not died. Or, at any rate, I believe she has made a complete and successful resurrection. She has been re-formed and re-fitted, and I am told that thus transformed she will be perfectly safe and a perfectly good vessel for^ the route. It was on these conditions that I entered into tire contract for the service.
Under Captain McClure?
I do not remember the name of the captain.

Is it the same contractor as in the case of the Lady Sybil?
SiT GEORGE FOSTER: I think not. They are Halifax people, who had the vessel and who have rebuilt her and have put her into what they say is excellent shape. She will be inspected, of course, and if she does not pass the inspection she will not go on. But this seemed the best we could get, and from the information we received I think she will perform the service all right.

That being the case, I have nothing more to say,	but I
would urge upon my hon. friend to have his eye upon that inspection, because it would be a very serious thing if any accident should happen. Mr. Leslie lost the contract with the Department of Trade and Commerce because he maintained the service with the Amelia, and Captain McClure from Pictou secured the Lady Sybil, which was specially built for that route. The Amelia was discarded and a new contract was entered upon. I hope that my hon. friend will see that the inspection is a good one.
Labour - Industrial Disputes Investigation Act-further amount required, $5,000.

Will my hon. friend
explain what became of his Bill amending the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act?

I had a draft Bill prepared about a year ago. A large number of copies were struck off and sent to persons throughout the country who were thought to be specially interested in the proposed amendments. My hon. friend got a copy.
I thought that we were suggesting some very practical amendments, which, in the interest of all concerned, should be enacted into' law, but the Bill was not introduced this session owing to the fact that some of the suggested amendments were considered controversial and their consideration would take up a good deal of time. I think I asked my hon. friend and some other3 whether or not they would agree to let the Bill go through with certain amendments, striking out any that they had serious objection to. An arrangement of that kind, however, was not effected, and the Bill was allowed to stand in order not to take up time which it was thought should be devoted to other purposes.

How does the question
stand with regard to the fair wage clause
in munition contracts? I see there has been quite an agitation in the country to extend the fair wage clause to the munition works.	.

The provisions of the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act have been extended to all industries in Canada manufacturing munitions of any kind. One reason why I am asking for an additional $5,000 is because I anticipate a larger number of boards of conciliation than there have been heretofore. The fair wage clause, I understand, is not being put in munition contracts. I took the matter up as soon as the war broke out, and I thought I had made an arrangement that such a clause should be inserted in every such contract. In fact, I was promised that that would be done. It was said, however, that a great many of these contracts were executed hurriedly in different parts of the country, sometimes by telegram, and it was .not thought practicable to have such clauses put in the contracts. Wherever any dispute has arisen, however, as to wages, or hours, or any other labour conditions, we have inquired into them and effected an adjustment, I think, in every case. There is not that advantage that some seem to think there is in having this clause in the contracts. In the case of the construction of a public building a schedule is prepared by the department, and contractors tendering for the job are supplied with copies of this schedule, so that they know exactly the wages they will have to pay to the different craftsmen employed in erecting the building. But where it is not known where the contract is to be executed; where it is not known whether the tender accepted will be from Vancouver or from Halifax, a' general clause is inserted simply requiring that the contractor, in executing the contract, shall pay the wages current in the district in which the contract is being executed. If any dispute arises in such cases we make investigation as to what the current rates are in the district. Although there is no such clause in the contracts for munitions, we take the same course; where any dispute arises we make an investigation as to the current rates of wages in the district where the contract is being carried out. So that we are taking the same course as if a clause of that kind were in the contract, and it works out just as advantageously to the workingman as if this clause had been inserted.
Can the minister tell me if Mr. Dubreuil, fair wage officer, has been replaced?

A gentleman named
N.arcisse Arcand, of Montreal, was appointed a few weeks ago.

Can the hon. minister give us any information as to the views of Mr. Lloyd -George on the question of the insertion of the fair wage clause in munition contracts? Is it true that Mr. Lloyd George intimated his willingness that the fair wage clause should be inserted in these contracts?
Mr. CROTHERS': I had no correspondence with Mr. Lloyd George. I understood the Prime Minister to say in the House that Lloyd George was not in favour of, having these clauses put in the contracts here in Canada.
Does the minister give the committee to understand that Mr. Lloyd George is opposed to having this clause inserted in the munition contracts?
That is my recollection of what the Prime Minister said in the House here. I am not quite sure that 1 am right in that, but that is my recollection.
My recollection is not the same. The minister follows these things closely; surely he is not depending for his information on what the Prime Minister or any one else says in the House.

I know that the Imperial Munitions Board, after inquiring into the matter, and after having, as I understand, some correspondence with Mr. Lloyd George, decided not to put in these clauses. I have that direct from the board.

In connection with people in works carried on by the Dominion ' Government employees, I think the minister was in the House when that matter was discussed. Perhaps the Minister of Labour would give an expression of his opinion on the question which I raised this afternoon of compensation to workmen employed on Government railways and in the Government elevators, workshops, etc., for injuries received in their employment.

I quite agree with my
hon. friend that those in the employ of this Government should be treated as generously as workmen are treated by private employers. As to the suggestion that they

should be paid according to the Compensation Act in force in each particular province, you might find that in one province a man could not recover under the Compensation Act of that province. The Ontario Act has been freed from any objection of that kind but there might be trouble in some other provinces. I think that the basis should be the salary or wages that a man is getting. My hon. friend spoke of the cost of living being higher in the extreme western provinces than in the East, and suggested that that might be taken into account. No rule has been adopted; each case has been considered on its own merits. I do not know of any case where a man has been injured or killed in the exercise of his duty where compensation has not been made if the facts were made known to us.

That may be true in
the case of death, that a compassionate allowance. is always voted; but I refer to cases of injury, such as the loss of fingers.

I do not remember
anything of that kind.
The-Workmen's Compensation Act would cover that, and my argument is that the workman should receive as generous treatment from the Government for injury as if he were working for some other person.

I quite agree with my hon. friend.
Quebec Harbour-River St. Charles-improvements to navigation, $700,000.

What is the
nature of the work you are doing in the St. Charles river?

This amount of $700,000
is required to carry on improvements, under contract with Messrs. Quinlan and Robertson. They comprise the construction of a concrete dam 1,600 feet long of an average height of 20 feet, and two locks, respectively 450 feet and 350 feet long, by 60 feet wide at the entrance walls, each lock having 15 feet of water on the sill at low water. The dam will have a super-structure of two lines of interlocked sheet piles, the whole hack filled with dredged material from the bed of the river. A sluiceway will be placed in the dam with gates to control the water in a pool to be created by the dam. An Order in Council was passed on the 12th of March, 1913, authorizing the .acceptance of the tender of Messrs. Quinlan and Robertson, of Montreal, for the construction of two

locks and dam in Quebec harbour, involving at the unit prices quoted therein an approximating expenditure of $1,873.80.
How far has the work advanced?

Just about one-third of
the work has been done.

Is the dam
completed, or does everything go on together?

The dam goes rather
ahead of the lock, and the dam is not quite completed yet.
Is it expected to have it completed during this season?

Yes. The dam will be
completed, but I do not know that all of the work will be completed.
This season?
Yes.
And the whole work will be completed next season?
I am satisfied it will.

I was told by a Quebecker-I do not vouch for the statement myself-that the effect of the dam and the locks would be to flood parts of the riverside, and that the city of Quebec, as a result, would have to change its sewerage system. Is there any correspondence between the department and the city of Quebec on that subject, and if a change has to be made in the sewerage system, will the cost fall upon the Government or upon the city? Perhaps that is a matter of detail with which my hon. friend is not familiar, but it was told to me by a gentleman who is not opposed to the project. He stated that the river St. Charles works were of such a character that the city would ultimately have to pay a very large sum of money to divert the present sewerage system from its present location.

I have some knowledge of the points the hon. member has mentioned. As a result of this work the question of the sewage of Quebec has been taken up by the engineer of Quebec, and the engineer of the Department of Public Works, and, while I am not clear as to the exact details, I understand that they have arrived at a solution of the matter, the cost, I think, being divided.
Between the city and the department?	.

Between the city and the department. I have not heard of any differences or conflicting views on the part of the engineers. I have not before me the exact arrangement, but I would be very glad to furnish it to my right hon. friend if he so desires.
Has the department not 'had the same trouble at Winnipeg in consequence of the dam at St. Andrew's rapids?

We have had to a greater or less extent. We had to do a considerable amount of dredging by reason of the filling in at Red river, and in connection with the sewage, too, to some extent. We have had practically the same difficulty there; the Government did the dredging and relieved the conditions.

I would be interested to know what is the arrangement which has been arrived at by the engineer of the city of Quebec and the engineer of the department. To. a layman like myself there seems to be no solution possible. The sewage cannot be diverted; it has to go into the St. Charles river because of the conformation of the land on which the city rests. The flow of the tide being obstructed, as it must be by the dam, 'as stated in the memorandum read by my hon. friend, a pool will be created which must collect all the sewage and all the mud that comes up from the river. I do not know how this can be overcome in any way.
I will be very glad to send the correspondence and everything we have in the department pertaining to the matter to my hon. friend.

Where the Government undertakes such a work as this and interferes with the sewage of a large city like Quebec, on what grounds does it expect that city, or any other city in a similar position, to pay part of the extra cost caused by the action of the Government? It does not seem to me to be fair to the city.

Of course, the ultimate completion of the work will be a great improvement in the district. It is a work which is regarded as being of great advantage to. the city of Quebec.
Air. A. W. CHISHOLA1:	There is an
item of $1,200 in the Main Estimates for repairs to the wharf at Broad Cove Marsh.

I would like to know the nature of this work.
Has any part of that amount been spent yet?

Nothing has been spent
yet.

I would like the minister to see that this work is done in the proper season. It appears that all the repairs in the county of Inverness are attended to in the fall of the year. It is an eyesore to see men repairing public works of this kind in November, when the climatic conditions are so bad. They cannot do the work effectively, and the result is that the department does not get value for its money. Very often the men cannot work more than five or six hours a day, and sometimes they cannot even work one hour a day. This occurred last year and the year before; I speak from . personal observation. I approve) of these repairs. They are very necessary because the wharf is in very bad shape.

The deputy informs me
that the work will go on as soon as possible.

There is an item for
Inverness Harbour, $15,000. Is it the intention to spend this amount this year, and what is the nature of the work?

I do not expect that we
shall find it necessary to go on with that this year. .

What does the minister propose to do in connection with Victoria harbour? There has been an investigation before the Public Accounts Committee, and

from the evidence adduced it would appear that over-payments have been made to a considerable extent, and that claims are in from the contractors for still larger amounts. According to the evidence given by the officers of the department, the amount of rock taken out was many times greater than the amount of rock there was to be taken out. I would like to know what the minister proposes to do in connection with that work.

If my hon. friend has
followed the evidence of the Public Accounts Committee he will have a knowledge of the facts. The engineer gave estimates for a greater quantity of rock to be taken out than had actually been taken out; at least that is the charge. So far as that is concerned, we are entirely protected. In the department we have ample funds in the shape of drawbacks and deposits to cover the loss. We have withheld a considerable sum of money and there will not be the loss of a dollar to the country in connection with the matter which has been before the Public Accounts Committee. When we first heard of the possibility of there being an over-estimate, Mr. Valiquette was sent out to British Columbia to investigate, and he did so. He reported that he did not think there had been any over-payment. There was still some doubt, and Mr. St. Laurent was sent out to make a further investigation. He went very carefully into all the circumstances, and his report went to show that there was a certain over-payment in connection with rock. But, whatever the over-payment, the department is amply protected, and will continue to be protected against over-payment on every classification.
What amount of rock will be paid for?

We have turned the matter over to the Exchequer Court, to adjust the differences between the engineers.
Public Works-French River-extension of breakwater pier, $2,000.
Mr. MoKENZIE: There are so many French rivers in Nova Scotia that I am wondering whether this is the one in my county.

Yes, it is. This vote of $2,000 is required for the construction of a breakwater 100 feet long, and from 16 to 20 feet wide. The district engineer estimates the cost as follows: 16,200 feet of cribwork at. 10 cents, $1,620.
Is that to stand tor this year?
Yes.
Will the same remark apply to the wharf at Plaster Mines?
Yes.
Is it proposed to go on with the boat harbour at Cape Dauphin this year?

We do not expect to go on with that this year.
Victoria harbour improvements, $1,000,000.

What is the proposed total expenditure at Victoria Harbour?
iMr. ROGERS: The contract with Sir John Jackson for the breakwater amounts to $1,797,000. The work has not been completed yet.
I think it was originally proposed to spend a larger amount than that for the harbour improvements there.

Besides the contract with Sir John Jackson there is the contract with Grant, Smith and Company, Limited, and Maedonnell for $2,444,000, for the construction of wharves.
Progress reported.
